summary.text: Phototropism is the growth of an organism in response to a light stimulus, most often seen in plants but also found in fungi.
Growth toward a light source is called positive phototropism, while growth away from light is called negative phototropism.
Auxin collects on the side away from the light, and the elongated cells there make the shoot curve toward the light.

items.prompt: A seedling on a windowsill bends toward the glass. Which side of its stem grows faster?

options.label: The window side, where the light speeds growth
The side away from the window, where cells elongate
Neither, as the lit side simply dries out
Both equally, and the stem then twists

items.explain: Auxin moves to the shaded side and promotes elongation of the cells there, which curves the plant toward the light.

items.prompt: A vine tip grows toward a dark, solid fence post and climbs it. What does this show?

options.label: Positive phototropism, because the post blocks the sun
The vine is ignoring light entirely
Negative phototropism, which lets some vine tips climb solid objects
Phototropism in a fungus

items.explain: Some vine shoot tips exhibit negative phototropism, which allows them to grow toward dark, solid objects and climb them.

items.prompt: On the shaded side of a shoot, cell walls loosen and water flows in. What starts this?

options.label: Auxin activating proton pumps that acidify the cell wall
Chloroplasts moving to the shaded side
Gravity pulling water toward the dark side
Light heating the dark side's walls directly

items.explain: Auxin activates proton pumps, which lowers the pH around the cell wall; expansins then loosen the walls and water enters the cells.

items.prompt: Where does a young shoot sense light, and where does it bend?

options.label: It senses at its base and bends at its tip
It senses in its middle and bends at its tip
It senses and bends only at its very tip
It senses at the tip, the coleoptile, and bends in its middle portion

items.explain: The coleoptile tip is necessary for light sensing, and the middle portion of the coleoptile is where the shoot curvature occurs.

items.prompt: Auxin has to pile up on one side of a shoot. Which proteins make it lopsided by moving auxin?

options.label: Phototropins, which carry auxin across cell walls
PIN proteins, with PIN3 as the main auxin carrier
Expansins, which ferry auxin to the shaded side
Proton pumps, which package auxin into vesicles

items.explain: PIN proteins are auxin transporters thought to polarize where auxin sits, and PIN3 is the primary auxin carrier. Phototropins receive light.

items.prompt: A houseplant's shoots lean toward a sunny window, and its leaves rearrange their chloroplasts. What do both achieve?

options.label: They maximize photosynthetic energy and promote growth
They keep the leaves cooler in the sun
They shield the plant from too much light
They make the plant grow toward darkness

items.explain: Most shoots show positive phototropism and rearrange chloroplasts in the leaves to maximize photosynthetic energy and promote growth.

Auxin moves toward the shaded side.

paragraphs.heading: Growing toward light
paragraphs.text: Phototropism is growth that responds to light, and it was once called heliotropism. It is seen most often in plants, though fungi and other organisms can show it too. It is one of many tropisms, the movements plants make in response to stimuli from outside. Growth toward a light source is called positive phototropism, and most plant shoots grow this way.

paragraphs.heading: Turning away
paragraphs.text: Growth away from light is called negative phototropism. Some vine shoot tips show it, which lets them grow toward dark, solid objects and climb them. It should not be confused with skototropism, which means growing toward darkness, whereas negative phototropism can mean either moving away from light or toward the dark. Phototropism works together with gravitropism so that a plant grows in the right direction.

paragraphs.heading: Auxin bends the shoot
paragraphs.text: The very tip of the shoot, called the coleoptile, is needed to sense the light, and the bend forms in its middle part. The Cholodny–Went hypothesis, from the early 20th century, predicts what happens when light falls from one side. A hormone called auxin moves to the shaded side and makes the cells there grow longer. With longer cells on the side away from the light, the plant curves toward the light source.

paragraphs.heading: How the cells stretch
paragraphs.text: Auxin switches on proton pumps, which lower the pH of cells on the dark side. This acid around the cell wall activates enzymes called expansins, which break hydrogen bonds in the wall and make it less rigid. The busier pumps also draw more dissolved substances into those cells, so water flows in along the osmotic gradient and turgor pressure, the pressure inside the cell, rises. Weaker walls and higher pressure make the cells swell, and that push drives the bending.

paragraphs.heading: Carriers that steer auxin
paragraphs.text: Proteins made from the PIN genes carry auxin and are thought to decide where it collects. PIN3 has been identified as the main carrier. Light-receiving proteins called phototropins may hold back an enzyme named PINOID kinase, which in turn boosts PIN3. Active PIN3 spreads auxin unevenly, so cells on one side of the stem lengthen more than on the other.

paragraphs.heading: Two light receptors
paragraphs.text: There are two main phototropins, phot1 and phot2. Plants lacking only phot2 still bend toward light like normal plants, but plants lacking both show no response at all. How much of each a plant has depends on its age and on how strong the light is. Whether the light is blue or red changes their levels too.
